gm_trajectory: Improving year-on-year purely on the metal price, compressing sequentially on unit costs: gross margin was 59.2% in the second quarter of 2026 on revenue of $579M, up from 54.2% a year earlier on revenue of $438M (revenue +32%), but down from 63.9% in the first quarter of 2026 - because the realised gold price fell from $4,829 to $4,504 per ounce while all-in sustaining costs rose from $1,862 to $1,728 guided upward for the full year to $1,775-1,875.
bull_thesis:
The case for Alamos rests on one genuinely exceptional asset and a balance sheet that can pay for its own growth. The Island Gold District in Ontario - the Island Gold underground mine feeding the larger Magino mill - is a top-tier Canadian ore body by any measure. Mineral reserves (ore the company has proven it can economically extract) nearly doubled during 2025 to over 8 million ounces, and the underground grade is 9.4 grams of gold per tonne, roughly ten times the open-pit grade beside it. Reserves across the whole company rose 32% to 16 million ounces, the seventh consecutive year of growth, and the mineral inventory at Island Gold has grown for ten straight years. This is a business that is much better at finding ore than the market gives it credit for.

The expansion study released in February 2026 is the spine of the bull case. Expanding the Magino mill to 20,000 tonnes a day by early 2028 is projected to take the district to an average of 534,000 ounces a year for a decade at mine-site all-in sustaining costs of $1,025 per ounce - more than double 2025 production at roughly 30% lower cost. Management put an after-tax net present value (the discounted worth of those future cash flows) of $8.2 billion on the district at a $3,200 gold price and $12 billion at $4,500. Add the Phase 3+ shaft at Island Gold, which reached its planned depth of 1,381 metres in the first quarter of 2026 with commissioning targeted for the first quarter of 2027, the PDA underground project in Mexico starting mid-2027, and the $920M Lynn Lake mine in Manitoba from 2029, and the company's stated path is roughly 800,000 ounces by 2028 and around 1 million ounces by 2030 - close to double today's output.

Crucially, none of this needs outside money. At 30 June 2026 Alamos held $675.9M of cash and short-term investments against $216M of total debt, a net cash position of about $420M, with $1.2 billion of total liquidity. It generated $352M of free cash flow in 2025 and $245.5M in the first half of 2026 while spending roughly $500M a year on growth. There is no equity issuance, no streaming deal, no dilution - the classic financing pattern that destroys shareholders in this sector is simply absent here.

The near-term problems are physical and, on the evidence, temporary. The June 2026 seismic events at Young-Davidson damaged an active mining front and cut mining rates from roughly 7,500 to about 5,000 tonnes a day; rehabilitation and enhanced ground support run through the second half of 2026, with management guiding to above 7,000 tonnes a day thereafter at an added $10-15M a year of sustaining capital - a real but small permanent cost. Meanwhile the flagship is delivering: Island Gold District produced a record 67,500 ounces in the second quarter of 2026, underground mining rates set records in both the first and second quarters and are on plan to reach 2,000 tonnes a day by year-end.

Insiders are voting with their own money - six open-market purchases totalling 65,000 shares against zero sales. The company raised its dividend 60% in February 2026, repurchased $50M of stock in the second quarter, and has eliminated 245,000 of the 330,000 ounces of below-market forward sales inherited with the Argonaut Gold acquisition, leaving only about 50,000 ounces hedged into 2027 - so shareholders now capture nearly the full gold price.

What must hold: gold needs to stay near or above $4,100 an ounce; the Phase 3+ shaft must commission on schedule in the first quarter of 2027; Young-Davidson must recover above 6,000 tonnes a day; and the Magino expansion must land in the first quarter of 2028 without a material capital overrun beyond the 4-5% inflation management has already flagged on the roughly $542M still to be spent. If those hold, 800,000 ounces in 2028 at even $1,450 per ounce of all-in sustaining cost - well above management's own $1,250 target - produces roughly $2.4 billion of annual mining margin, and the shares are worth multiples of today's price.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that the ore body is bad. It is that the market is already paying a premium price for promises this management has failed to keep five times in eight quarters, into a falling gold tape, with the cost base moving the wrong way.

Start with the delivery record, because it is the heart of it. In February 2026 Alamos guided 2026 to a 12% production increase at all-in sustaining costs of $1,500-1,600 per ounce. On 29 July 2026 that had become production of 510,000-560,000 ounces - roughly 2% *below* 2025 - at costs of $1,775-1,875 per ounce. The growth year was erased and the cost guide moved 17% above a 2025 result of $1,524 that had itself already missed. That follows 2025, when cost guidance was raised 12% in July, production guidance cut 6% in October, and the full year still came in below the reduced target. Management asserted in October 2025 that 'we pride ourselves on providing consistently accurate guidance' in the same breath as a cut. Between late June and July 2026, three law firms - Pomerantz, Schall and Bronstein Gewirtz - opened investigations into whether the company's statements about Young-Davidson were misleading. No wrongdoing has been established and no complaint has been filed, but the headline and legal-cost overhang is real.

Second, the valuation. The shares are down roughly 48% from a 52-week high of $55.41, which looks like distress but is not cheapness. Against peers, Alamos trades at about 6.7 times trailing operating profit on a figure inflated by the $227M Turkish asset-sale gain - closer to 8 times on clean forward numbers at spot gold - with a free-cash-flow yield of only 2.6%. Kinross, with a near-identical 2026 cost guide of about $1,730 per ounce, trades at 4.7 times with a 10.9% free-cash-flow yield and a 25.2% return on invested capital against Alamos's 14.8%. Agnico Eagle, materially lower cost at $1,400-1,550 and with a far better execution record, trades at 7.1 times with a 5.8% yield. Investors are paying Agnico-like multiples for third-quartile costs and a broken guidance record. The share price has fallen a long way; the valuation has not fallen with it.

Third, the cost bridge that nobody has audited. The entire case requires all-in sustaining costs to fall from roughly $1,825 today to about $1,250 in 2028 - a 31% unit-cost decline. Management itself describes 4-6% labour and contractor inflation, has added an unbudgeted Canadian retention programme worth about $30 per ounce that continues into 2027, and has made enhanced ground support 'the standard going forward in the lower mine' at Young-Davidson. Note too that the $1,025 per ounce headline for the expanded district is a *mine-site* figure, which excludes corporate overhead - the consolidated number shareholders actually receive will be higher. No analyst on any of these five calls has forced management to bridge that gap line by line.

Fourth, and most immediate, the commodity torque cuts both ways. Alamos has a two-year beta to gold of 1.73 - it moves roughly 1.7 times as much as the metal. Gold is already down about 26% from its January 2026 peak near $5,600 to roughly $4,100. On the honest, uncontaminated second-quarter margin, a further 10% fall in gold takes roughly 15% off operating profit - about $220M a year off a $1.47 billion base. Because free cash flow is what is left after roughly $500M a year of growth capital and about $250-330M of cash taxes, that same $220M is more than half of the roughly $390M of annual free cash flow the company generates at spot. At $3,700 gold, free cash flow approaches breakeven while $920M of Lynn Lake construction and about $542M of remaining Magino expansion capital still have to be funded. The net cash cushion of $420M - about $1.00 a share - is comfortable, not a fortress.

Fifth, capital allocation has been pro-cyclical at exactly the wrong moments. Alamos repurchased $50M of stock in the second quarter of 2026 at an average $35.70 per share, now 19% underwater, and spent $92.3M eliminating 35,000 ounces of hedges at $4,458 per ounce with spot now near $4,100. Both were defensible decisions; both were made near the top.

What would confirm the bear case: a third guidance revision at the third-quarter results in late October 2026; Young-Davidson still below 6,000 tonnes a day at year-end; any walk-back of the 800,000-ounce 2028 target in the year-end three-year guidance update management has explicitly promised; slippage of the Phase 3+ shaft beyond the first quarter of 2027; or gold breaking below $3,700 an ounce.

peer_comps_note: Measured against the assigned true competitors, Alamos is the expensive one. On trailing figures as of 4 August 2026: Alamos trades at 6.7 times operating profit with a 2.6% free-cash-flow yield and a 14.8% return on invested capital; Kinross Gold at 4.7 times with a 10.9% free-cash-flow yield and a 25.2% return on invested capital; Agnico Eagle at 7.1 times with a 5.8% free-cash-flow yield and a 15.7% return. The Alamos multiple is additionally flattered - its trailing operating profit includes the $227M after-tax gain on the Turkish asset sale, so the clean forward figure at spot gold is nearer 8 times. On unit costs for 2026 the ranking is unambiguous: Agnico Eagle $1,400-1,550 per ounce, Kinross about $1,730, Alamos $1,775-1,875, IAMGOLD $1,775-1,925, Eldorado Gold $2,465 in the second quarter of 2026. Alamos therefore sits in the sector's third cost quartile while carrying a first-quartile valuation. Kinross is the sharpest comparison: near-identical cost position, roughly four times the free-cash-flow yield. The premium Alamos commands is entirely a growth premium for the 2028-2030 Island Gold ramp - which is real, but which has now slipped twice, and which the peer set does not require you to pay for.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about the ore body - it is about the discount rate the market applies to this management's promises.

First, the published street view is a fossil. The consensus price target of $51 is built from five targets set over the past year, most of them struck when gold was near $5,000 an ounce and before the guidance cut. Only one target has printed in the last quarter: RBC Capital's $42 on 9 July 2026, when the stock was $29.68 - and even that predates the 29 July guidance revision. So the $51 headline is not a street-wide view at all; it is the residue of a tape that no longer exists. Any investor anchoring to it is anchoring to gold at $5,000.

Second, and more substantively, the market is still pricing Alamos as a low-cost grower. It trades near 8 times forward operating profit at spot gold with a 2.6% free-cash-flow yield, versus Kinross - whose 2026 cost guide of about $1,730 per ounce is essentially identical to Alamos's $1,775-1,875 - at 4.7 times with a 10.9% yield. Investors are paying roughly a 70% premium to a same-cost peer for a growth pipeline. That premium was earned when the pipeline was on schedule. It has now slipped twice: Lynn Lake from late 2028 to 2029 with a conceded 15% capital increase, and the 2026 production year from a promised 12% increase to a roughly 2% decrease.

Third, the specific assumption that is factually wrong. Sell-side models bridge from today to 800,000 ounces in 2028 at roughly $1,250 per ounce of all-in sustaining cost. They model the ounces, which the mine plan genuinely supports - higher-grade Island Gold underground ore displacing lower-grade Magino open-pit feed does mechanically lower unit costs. What they under-model is the base those costs start from. The 2026 guide moved to $1,775-1,875. Getting to $1,250 is a 31% unit-cost decline delivered against management's own disclosed 4-6% labour and contractor inflation, a new unbudgeted Canadian retention programme worth about $30 per ounce that runs into 2027, and permanently higher ground support at Young-Davidson worth $10-15M a year. Note also that the headline $1,025 per ounce for the expanded Island Gold District is a mine-site figure that excludes corporate overhead; the consolidated number will be higher still.

Fourth, where we agree with the market and it is worth saying plainly: the reserve growth is real and audited - 32% higher to 16 million ounces, seven consecutive years - and Island Gold at 9.4 grams per tonne is genuinely one of the better underground ore bodies in Canada. Our disagreement is about price and timing, not quality. The correct posture is to want to own this asset, at a materially lower price.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are where the margin gets squeezed from both ends simultaneously, and there is no cash-flow cushion being built while it happens.

The realised gold price is falling as reported costs rise. Alamos realised $4,829 an ounce in the first quarter of 2026 and $4,504 in the second; spot is now near $4,100 and futures near $4,158. So the third and fourth quarters will be sold into a price roughly 9% below the second quarter's - while guided all-in sustaining costs move up to $1,775-1,875 from a second-quarter actual of $1,728. First-half free cash flow of $245.5M was earned at prices that will not repeat; second-half free cash flow will plausibly land nearer $120-160M. Full-year free cash flow of roughly $380-400M at spot has to cover about $68M of dividends, continued buybacks, and roughly $500M a year of growth capital. It broadly works at $4,100 gold. It does not work at $3,700.

The operating repair is unfinished. Young-Davidson is running near 5,000 tonnes a day against a roughly 7,500 tonne design, with rehabilitation and enhanced ground support running through the whole of the second half. Management guides to above 7,000 tonnes a day thereafter, but on the 30 July call the chief operating officer would not commit to a step change - 'we will be looking to provide further clarity to that by the end of the year.' La Yaqui Grande in Mexico is leaching more slowly than planned, pushing ounces from 2026 into 2027. Island Gold underground must still climb from 1,550 to 2,000 tonnes a day by year-end to hit even the reduced guidance.

The third-quarter result in late October 2026 is the pressure point. It will be the third consecutive quarter carrying bad operating news, and the market has already shown how it reacts - the shares fell about 12% on 22 June 2026 on the seismic disclosure alone. A third guidance revision, or a fourth-quarter that requires a heroic ramp to hit even 510,000 ounces, is a live possibility.

There is no debt wall - that is the genuine comfort. Long-term debt is only $200M against $675.9M of cash and short-term investments, and total liquidity is about $1.2 billion. Alamos is not going to be forced into anything. But it is committing roughly $1.5 billion of growth capital across 2026-2029 - Lynn Lake at $920M with no production until 2029, and about $542M still to spend on the Magino expansion with management conceding 4-5% inflation on it - into a gold price that has already fallen 26% from its January peak.

Finally, the legal overhang. Pomerantz, the Schall Law Firm and Bronstein Gewirtz all opened investigations between late June and July 2026 into the Young-Davidson disclosures. These are law-firm-initiated investigations, not filed complaints and not regulatory actions, and no wrongdoing has been established - but they generate recurring negative headlines and could turn into a filed class action, which typically adds legal cost and caps the multiple until resolved.
positioning_washout:
This is not a dividend-cut story, so the classic yield-holder liquidation does not apply. The dividend was raised 60% in February 2026 to $0.04 a share quarterly, costs roughly $68M a year, and is comfortably covered even in the adverse case. Nothing forces income holders out.

The mechanical selling comes from two other directions. The first is passive and generalist gold exposure. Alamos is a meaningful weight in the gold-miner exchange-traded funds and in generalist precious-metals funds, and it carries a two-year beta to gold of 1.73 - it moves roughly 1.7 times the metal. With gold down about 26% from its January 2026 peak near $5,600, those vehicles have been redeeming, and redemptions sell Alamos in proportion to its index weight regardless of what the ore body is worth. That flow is indiscriminate and it is not finished while gold is falling.

The second is a mandate handover. The shareholders who owned Alamos owned the 800,000-ounces-by-2028 story - it was a growth holding in a commodity sector, and it won a TSX30 award in 2025 for a 310% three-year share-price gain. The 29 July guidance cut broke that story: the promised 12% growth year became a roughly 2% decline. Growth mandates do not hold a company that has just cancelled its growth year; they sell it to value mandates, and that rotation typically takes two to three quarters and caps every rally in between. The shares are already 48% below their 52-week high of $55.41 and trade below both the 50-day average of $33.08 and the 200-day average of $38.85, which is the visual signature of exactly that handover in progress.

There are two genuine offsets. Insiders have bought - six open-market purchases totalling 65,000 shares, zero sales - which is the honest version of the signal, excluding grants. And the company itself is a buyer, having repurchased $50M in the second quarter, with management stating on 30 April that 'given the opportunity we see now with our shares underperforming... we expect to be more active with the share buyback.' That said, the second-quarter repurchases were executed at an average $35.70 a share and are now about 19% underwater, so the corporate bid has not been price-sensitive.

The capitulation trigger to watch for is specific: a third guidance revision at the third-quarter results in late October, or a walk-back of the 2028 targets in the year-end three-year guidance update. Either would be the moment the last growth holders leave, and it is the most likely place a genuine wash-out low prints.
forcing_function:
Three dated corporate events will settle this, and the second is by far the most important.

1. Third-quarter 2026 results, expected late October 2026. The first clean quarter under the reduced guidance. The specific numbers that matter: whether Young-Davidson mining rates have recovered above 6,000 tonnes a day from the roughly 5,000 they have been running since the June seismic events, whether all-in sustaining costs land inside the new $1,775-1,875 range rather than above it, and whether Island Gold underground has continued climbing from 1,550 tonnes a day toward the 2,000 target. This is the credibility test - a fifth consecutive quarter of downward revision would confirm that the forecasting problem is systematic rather than circumstantial.

2. The year-end 2026 three-year guidance update, promised explicitly by the chief operating officer on the 30 July 2026 call: 'we will be looking to provide further clarity to that by the end of the year as part of our 3-year guidance.' This is the single most consequential disclosure in the story, because it is where management either reaffirms or retreats from 800,000 ounces in 2028 at roughly $1,250 per ounce of all-in sustaining cost. Every dollar of the premium the shares carry over Kinross rests on that target. Reaffirming it with a credible cost bridge - showing exactly how they get from $1,825 to $1,250 through higher-grade Island Gold ore displacing Magino open-pit feed - forces a re-rating upward. Cutting it, or pushing 2028 to 2029, takes the shares toward the adverse case.

3. Commissioning of the Phase 3+ shaft at Island Gold, targeted for the first quarter of 2027 and reaffirmed on 30 July 2026. The shaft reached its planned depth of 1,381 metres in the first quarter of 2026, all rock work is complete, and remaining work is shaft furnishing plus the underground ore and waste handling infrastructure at the 1,350-metre level. This is the event that mechanically lowers Island Gold's unit costs by replacing truck haulage with skipping, and it is the most de-risked item on the list - roughly 100% of its growth capital is spent or committed.

Beyond those, the Magino mill expansion to 20,000 tonnes a day is targeted for the first quarter of 2028 with about $542M still to spend, and Lynn Lake's first production is targeted for 2029. Both are too distant to force anything in the next year, but slippage in either would compound the credibility problem.
moderator_conclusion:
Wait for the wash-out. Alamos owns a genuinely excellent ore body attached to a company that cannot yet be trusted to forecast it, and at $28.91 the market is still paying a growth premium for a growth year that was cancelled five days ago.

Start with what is true. The Island Gold District in Ontario is one of the better underground gold assets in Canada - over 8 million ounces of reserves after nearly doubling in 2025, 9.4 grams of gold per tonne underground, open laterally and to depth beyond 1.6 kilometres, with an expanded mill plan that management projects will deliver 534,000 ounces a year for a decade. Company-wide reserves rose 32% to 16 million ounces, the seventh straight year of growth. The balance sheet is clean: $675.9M of cash and short-term investments against $216M of debt, about $420M of net cash, no maturity wall, no equity issuance and no streaming deal. Insiders have bought in the open market six times and sold nothing. On the forensic dimensions that kill investors in this sector - serial dilution, promoter financing, fabricated backlog - Alamos is clean. That is why this is a 'wait', not a 'pass'.

Now what is priced. On cost-curve position the deterministic proxy in our own inputs is misleading and must be corrected: its 79.3% operating margin absorbs the $227M Turkish asset-sale gain, and the clean second-quarter figure is 68.5%. The company's own reported all-in sustaining cost of $1,728 an ounce, guided to $1,775-1,875 for 2026, puts Alamos in the sector's third cost quartile - above Agnico Eagle at $1,400-1,550 and above Kinross at about $1,730 - not the low-cost tier the narrative implies. Yet on valuation Alamos is the most expensive of the three: roughly 8 times forward operating profit at spot gold with a 2.6% free-cash-flow yield, against Kinross at 4.7 times and 10.9% with an essentially identical cost structure. A same-cost peer offers four times the cash yield. The premium is a growth premium, and the growth has slipped twice.

On contracting and reserve life, the position is solid and improving: 16 million ounces of reserves against roughly 535,000 ounces of annual production is a reserve life near thirty years, the hedge book inherited from Argonaut Gold has been reduced from 330,000 to about 50,000 ounces so shareholders now capture nearly the full spot price, and there is no problematic offtake obligation. On capital discipline the record is more mixed than the story: management sensibly declined to chase acquisitions in July 2026, but it repurchased $50M of stock at $35.70 a share (now 19% underwater) and paid $92.3M to buy out hedges at $4,458 an ounce with gold now near $4,100 - both defensible when made, both made near the top. And it is committing roughly $1.5 billion of growth capital through 2029 into a metal that has already fallen 26% from its January peak.

On the regime and the torque, which must be stated symmetrically: precious metals read as neutral, not favourable. Gold at roughly $4,100 sits below its 200-day average of $4,587 and 26% below the January 2026 peak. Alamos moves about 1.7 times the metal. On the honest margin, a further 10% fall in gold removes roughly 15% of operating profit - about $220M a year - which is more than half of the roughly $390M of free cash flow the company generates at spot, because free cash flow is only what survives after $500M a year of growth spending. That is the number the bull case has to hold against, and it is why the adverse value is $17 rather than something comfortable. The same torque adds 15% on the way up, which is why the favourable value is $43. We judge the miner, not the metal chart - and the miner's problem is that its costs rose 17% in the same twelve months its revenue per ounce rose 40%.

Reconciling: base-case fair value is $26 a share, roughly 10% below today's price. The favourable case at $43 requires gold at $4,500 and clean execution; the adverse case at $17 requires gold at $3,700 and Young-Davidson still constrained. Buying at $28.91 means paying above conservative fair value for the right to underwrite a 31% unit-cost reduction from a management team that has revised guidance downward five times in eight quarters, with three law firms investigating its disclosures. That is the wrong price for that risk.

The specific level: below $22 a share - roughly 0.55 times net asset value, about 18% upside to base fair value against 23% downside - this becomes an easy allocation.
